Costs: Leaks 2 L of water per turn
Risks / What Can Happen: Short-circuit if placed too close to the Energy card
Lore: Consumer-grade polymer containers (COTS) are not certified for aerospace: porosity, chemical leaching into drinking water and poor resistance to launch vibrations.

Risks / What Can Happen: Contamination risk: crew gets sick, and sickness means excessive water consumption
Lore: Recovering water from celestial bodies (In-Situ Resource Utilization, ISRU) is a key path for Mars and asteroid missions, but extraterrestrial ice carries heavy metals, chemical pollutants and abrasive dust. Drunk unfiltered it makes the crew ill, and ill crew members drink more.

Costs: -15 Morale (noise of an old piston coffee maker, insomnia in the bedroom)
Risks / What Can Happen: If Energy suffers a voltage drop, boiling stops halfway and contaminates the freeze-dried Food reserves (-15 Food)
Synergy / Impact: Depends on Energy; can damage Food
Lore: Real stations recover drinking water from crew urine by distillation (ISS Urine Processor Assembly). This 1982-vintage unit does the job but is loud, temperamental and very sensitive to power fluctuations.

Risks / What Can Happen: Risk of the crew falling sick
Lore: Based on ISS water-processing technology: multifiltration beds and a catalytic reactor strip organic contaminants from wastewater. Saturated or imperfect beds let residues through, which makes the crew ill, and ill crew members drink more.

Gives: +5 L water per turn (recovered from crew sweat and breathing)
Lore: Exhaled air and sweat load the cabin with humidity. Space environmental control systems (CDRA, condensing heat exchangers) condense this humidity and redirect it to the drinking water reserves.

Gives: +X L water (variable, can be a lot)
Lore: Unlike chlorine (unstable and corrosive in space), NASA uses silver ions or iodine to disinfect stored water aboard spacecraft without permanently harming astronaut health.

Gives: Infinite water (+X L). No risk of illness
Synergy / Impact: Neutralizes odor/contamination maluses from the Food domain. Trades Oxygen for Water
Lore: A far-future extrapolation of ISS humidity-condensing technology: the cabin atmosphere becomes an endless water source and every drop is purified to a standard that rules out waterborne illness. Running the system draws oxygen from the cabin air, so the crew pays for endless water in daily oxygen.

Risks / What Can Happen: Malfunctions randomly every 3 turns: module plunges into darkness and communications are cut
Lore: Off-the-shelf components that are not radiation-hardened suffer rapid semiconductor degradation under the Van Allen radiation belts.

Costs: Very heavy: weight penalty on the rocket (inventory)
Lore: Lead-acid batteries are extremely heavy and present major chemical risks in case of leaks in microgravity, which bans them from crewed spaceflight standards.

Risks / What Can Happen: 30% chance of causing a cabin fire and burning Food
Synergy / Impact: Links two Energy cards; can damage Food
Lore: Electrical circuit overloading is one of the most feared fire risks aboard space stations because of air confinement and the circulation of pure oxygen.

Risks / What Can Happen: Fragile: may break during the run
Lore: Modern Li-ion batteries used by NASA rely on sophisticated thermal management systems (BMS) to prevent thermal runaway, a critical risk in space. Even so, they are delicate: one damaged cell can end the battery's life mid-mission.

Costs: Crew exercises to generate it: consumes more Food and more Oxygen
Lore: Human-powered generation: the crew pedals to feed the grid. Stations already use cycle ergometers for exercise (ISS CEVIS), and a working body burns extra calories and breathes more oxygen.
Photovoltaic arrays are the standard power source of crewed spacecraft (ISS solar array wings). Large deployable arrays add mass and launch constraints.
Used by NASA deep space probes (Curiosity, Perseverance, Voyager) when solar panels are ineffective. It converts the heat of plutonium-238 decay into electricity via the Seebeck effect.

Gives: Very large amount of energy. No risk of energy failure
Lore: Developed by NASA, the Kilopower project aims to provide a lightweight and reliable nuclear power source for future crewed bases on the Moon or Mars.

Game conceit: a water loop is filled once, then pumped endlessly through a turbine. Real spacecraft already rely on pumped fluid loops (ISS thermal control system), and the one-time water cost is what the crew pays to start it.

Costs: Heavy: takes 2 inventory slots. Permanent -5% Morale (noisy leaks)
Lore: High-pressure tanks stored without maintenance risk metal fatigue and slow leaks. In space, managing gas mixes (oxygen/nitrogen) prevents hypoxia and toxic hyperoxia.

Risks / What Can Happen: If Water runs short (below X L) the plant dies and production stops
Synergy / Impact: Competes with the crew for the Water supply
Lore: Plants produce oxygen through photosynthesis, but at spacecraft scale the yield is negligible against human metabolic needs.

Costs: Draws a lot of Energy. Loud: crew rest is worse (-5% Morale per turn)
Synergy / Impact: Raises the load on the Energy domain
Lore: Terrestrial concentrators pull oxygen out of cabin air with molecular sieves. They are power-hungry and were never designed for microgravity or continuous operation.
The ISS OGA splits water into hydrogen and oxygen by electrolysis. The leftover hydrogen can be combined with exhaled CO2 in a Sabatier reaction.
The ISS stores oxygen and nitrogen in external high-pressure tanks, topped up by resupply missions. They are used to repressurize the station and as a buffer when production drops.

Gives: Infinite oxygen. Special buff: recycles CO2 and returns +25% Water
Synergy / Impact: Perfect synergy with Food (algae biomass) and Water
Lore: An ideal closed loop studied for autonomous Martian habitats. Microbial bioreactors and chemical catalysts purify the air and regenerate water.
